```{r setup, include=FALSE}
script <- if (file.exists("R/run_project.R")) {
  "R/run_project.R"
} else {
  "blog/posts/post2/R/run_project.R"
}
source(script)
analysis <- post2_result$analysis
d <- analysis$data
sources <- post2_result$sources
get_row <- function(id) d[d$id == id, ]
ds <- get_row("data-scientists")
ec <- get_row("economists")
op <- get_row("operations-research-analysts")
ma <- get_row("management-analysts")
mr <- get_row("market-research-analysts")
fa <- get_row("financial-analysts")
money <- function(x) scales::dollar(x, accuracy = 1)
count <- function(x) scales::comma(x, accuracy = 1)
period <- paste0(ds$projection_start, "-", ds$projection_end)
post_dir <- dirname(dirname(normalizePath(script, winslash = "/")))
# The prose interprets this archived snapshot. Review it if inputs change.
if (ds$growth_pct != max(d$growth_pct) ||
    ec$median_pay_usd != max(d$median_pay_usd) ||
    ma$annual_openings != max(d$annual_openings) ||
    ma$experience == "None" ||
    !setequal(d$id[d$priority_screen],
              c("data-scientists", "operations-research-analysts"))) {
  stop("The inputs change the findings. Review the article before publishing.")
}
```

An economics student opens a job site. Should the first saved search be “economist,” “financial analyst,” or “data scientist”? Each can involve quantitative work, but choosing where to look requires more than finding a familiar title. **Which occupations offer a useful starting point when weighing pay, growth, and the volume of openings?**

I use R's `rvest` package to extract six deliberately selected [Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational profiles](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/). They help compare job markets. They cannot show which occupation an economics graduate is most likely to enter.

## A job category is not an academic background

A financial analyst may have an economics degree, use economic models, and describe themselves as an economist. That does not make the BLS categories interchangeable. The [Standard Occupational Classification](https://www.bls.gov/soc/2018/soc_2018_class_prin_cod_guide.pdf) assigns jobs according to work performed, with rules for mixed duties. Academic background and professional identity can cross those boundaries.

Here, “economists” means SOC **19-3011**, while the financial-analysts profile combines **13-2051** (financial and investment analysts) and **13-2054** (financial risk specialists). The code records all component codes and checks that none appears in two comparison rows. Financial analysts' combined statistics stay combined; a median cannot be split into subgroup medians.

**These are occupational comparisons, not six exclusive groups of economics-trained people.** I neither add the opening counts into a total for economics graduates nor interpret wage differences as the payoff from choosing one career over another.

## Fast growth and many openings tell different stories

In the archived profiles, data scientists lead projected growth at **`r ds$growth_pct`%**, versus **`r ec$growth_pct`%** for the economist occupation over `r period`. Their median annual pay, `r money(ds$median_pay_usd)`, is close to economists' `r money(ec$median_pay_usd)`. That combination makes data science worth examining for a student who enjoys computation.

```{r growth-chart, fig.cap="Projected employment growth by BLS occupational profile. Teal marks profiles passing the stated preference screen, not an official BLS rating.", fig.alt="Horizontal bars compare projected growth across six occupational profiles, with data scientists highest. Teal highlights data science and operations research under the stated preference screen.", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.8}
analysis$growth_plot
```

The openings chart changes the emphasis. Management analysts have about `r count(ma$annual_openings)` projected openings annually, market research analysts `r count(mr$annual_openings)`, and data scientists `r count(ds$annual_openings)`. The economist category has `r count(ec$annual_openings)`.

Growth measures expansion relative to an occupation's existing size. Openings also include replacement needs when workers leave an occupation or retire. A large, slower-growing occupation can therefore generate more openings than a small, fast-growing one. These counts cover all qualifying workers, not positions reserved for economics graduates.

```{r openings-chart, fig.cap="Projected average annual openings by BLS occupational profile. Counts include replacement needs and all experience levels; they are not current vacancies.", fig.alt="Horizontal bars compare projected annual openings across six occupational profiles. Management analysts have the largest count and economists the smallest.", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.8}
analysis$openings_plot
```

## A shortlist to investigate, not a promise of employment

Suppose a student wants median pay of at least **$85,000**, projected growth of at least **10%**, and no typical requirement for related work experience. This preference screen selects data scientists and operations research analysts. The latter offer `r money(op$median_pay_usd)` median pay, `r op$growth_pct`% growth, and about `r count(op$annual_openings)` annual openings.

```{r comparison-table}
knitr::kable(analysis$comparison_table,
  caption = paste0("Selected occupational profiles. Pay: May ", ds$pay_year,
    "; projections: ", period, ". Source: BLS OOH. Financial analysts combine two SOC codes."))
```

For this student, create saved searches in those two areas, then check each posting's tasks and qualifications. BLS lists bachelor's-level entry education for both; this does not mean an economics degree alone supplies every technical skill. Management analysis offers more openings but typically requires related experience, so a new graduate should look specifically for campus or entry-level programs.

The rule also excludes financial analysis despite its `r money(fa$median_pay_usd)` median pay, because its `r fa$growth_pct`% growth misses the chosen cutoff. That is a consequence of the preference rule, not evidence that finance is a poor choice. Raising the pay floor to $90,000 or growth floor to 15% leaves only data science. A saved nine-scenario table shows how the shortlist changes.

## What the comparison can—and cannot—decide

Median pay is not a starting salary. National projections do not reveal local vacancies, competition, visa eligibility, or an applicant's hiring probability. The six profiles are a selected comparison, and their workers differ in skills and experience.

**The takeaway is to use occupational evidence to choose searches, then use actual job descriptions to decide where to apply.** Under the stated preferences, data science and operations research are starting points. Shared economics training does not make the categories identical—or establish that either is the best path for every graduate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Sources, scraping, and replication

The six archived Summary HTML fragments were captured September 20, 2026. Pay refers to May `r ds$pay_year`; projections cover `r period`. The original capture method and file hashes are recorded in `data/raw/manifest.csv`. The numerical inputs are extracted from those HTML files with `rvest`, not manually copied into the comparison table.

```{r source-links, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(sources))) {
  cat(sprintf("- [%s](%s)\n", sources$occupation[i], sources$url[i]))
}
```

The [SOC definitions](https://www.bls.gov/soc/2018/soc_2018_definitions.pdf) and [classification rules](https://www.bls.gov/soc/2018/soc_2018_class_prin_cod_guide.pdf) document the distinction between jobs and backgrounds. `data/occupation_scope.csv` is author-documented classification metadata, separate from scraped numbers. The financial profile's Employment Projections table identifies its two component occupations. Classification documentation was checked October 8, 2026.

Extraction targets the Quick Facts table and the Summary's annual-openings paragraph. Cleaning removes whitespace, commas, dollar signs, and descriptive text; validation checks unique profiles, numerical fields, common measurement years, archived-file integrity, and nonoverlapping SOC coverage.

Rendering reuses saved HTML without sending new requests. The optional collector reads current robots rules, waits between six public-page requests, and stops on access errors. No login, paywall, CAPTCHA, or other restriction is bypassed. Live collection is optional because it cannot reproduce the original snapshot if pages change.

From the website root, run `source("blog/posts/post2/setup.R")` once, then `source("blog/posts/post2/R/run_project.R")`. Render `blog/posts/post2/index.qmd` and `blog/index.qmd`. See the [Post 2 README](https://github.com/augenstern118/testrepo/tree/main/blog/posts/post2) for exact commands, a file map, and output definitions.
:::
